title: PanMETAI - a high performance tabular foundation model for accurate pancreatic cancer diagnosis via NMR metabolomics

paper_content.abstract: Late diagnosis and the lack of effective early detection techniques contribute to the poor prognosis of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). To address this challenge, we develop 1H NMR-based metabolomics–AI platforms employing customized multilayer support vector machine (SVM), AutoGluon, and Tabular Foundation Model (TabPFN) frameworks. These platforms integrate serum metabolomic profiles—including small-molecule metabolites and lipoproteins—with clinical/biochemical parameters (age, CA19-9) and Activin A, derived from 902 participants (424 high-risk controls and 478 PDAC cases). Our TabPFN-based algorithm, PanMETAI, outperform state-of-the-art models. In the Taiwanese training and validation cohort, the model achieved an impressive AUC of 0.99 (95% CI: 0.98–0.99). Its robustness is further confirmed in a Lithuanian external validation cohort (n = 322), which yields an AUC of 0.93 (0.90-0.95). Notably, it identifies key signature patterns that improve early-stage (I/II) PDAC diagnosis and perform well with small sample sizes (n = 50). TabPFN-PanMETAI offers a rapid, accurate, and non-invasive tool for early PDAC detection, with strong potential for clinical application.
paper_content.introduction:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a highly lethal malignancy with a dismal 13% 5-year survival rate1, primarily due to late-stage diagnosis2, underscoring a critical unmet need for reliable early detection as current diagnostic approaches lack sufficient specificity and sensitivity3–5. The serological biomarker, carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9)6,7, exhibits limited utility due to its elevated levels in various nonmalignant conditions8,9, rendering it insufficient as a standalone diagnostic marker. Despite extensive studies have explored alternative PDAC biomarkers—including liquid biopsy approaches using protein and gene markers10, cell-free DNA11, microRNAs12, and exosomes13—limitations in large-scale validation and clinical superiority over CA19-9 persist. As a result, current biomarkers remain inadequate for accurate, rapid, and cost-effective PDAC diagnosis in clinical settings.

Metabolomics, the study of metabolites and lipids within biological systems, offers a promising strategy for discovering PDAC biomarkers14,15. Disrupted metabolic homeostasis is increasingly recognized as a key contributor to PDAC tumorigenesis16,17. Several studies have identified metabolic and lipidomic biomarkers with potential diagnostic value18–21. However, reliance on a limited set of biomarkers is insufficient to capture the full complexity of PDAC and often suffers from issues of validation or reproducibility. This limits their effectiveness in distinguishing early-stage patients, particularly in high-risk populations, underscoring the need for a more comprehensive and robust diagnostic approach.

This study introduces a powerful approach to improve early detection of PDAC using high-resolution proton nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy. We generated comprehensive, label-free serum metabolomic fingerprints and integrated these with clinical/biochemical parameters and a prognostic protein biomarker to develop a multilayer diagnostic framework. This approach overcomes the limitations of conventional biomarker-driven methods by enabling practical interpretation of complex NMR spectra and integrating heterogeneous data to enhance early-stage cancer detection accuracy.

We leveraged recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) to evaluate the diagnostic performance of several state-of-the-art models, including the transformer-based neural network (Tabular Foundation Model) TabPFN22 and the AutoGluon AutoML platforms23. Through systematic optimization, we established a fast, effective, and highly accurate algorithm, PanMETAI (a TabPFN-based algorithm integrating NMR metabolomics, age, CA19-9, and Activin A) for PDAC detection.
paper_content.results:
Developing machine learning approaches for enhanced pancreatic cancer detection using metabolic features, Age, CA19-9, and Activin A

An overview of the study design is presented in Fig. 1. Serum samples from 350 participants in the exploration cohort (Table 1) and 552 participants in the validation cohorts (Table 2) were divided into three datasets for machine learning (ML) development and validation (Fig. 1A). To simulate a clinically challenging diagnostic setting, we adopted a structured data-splitting strategy to train a generalized ML model. The first cohort was divided into a training dataset [n = 200; 100 high-risk controls (HRC) and 100 patients with stage I/II PDAC] and a developing (validation) test dataset (n = 150; 50 HRC and 100 patients with stage III/IV PDAC). The second cohort was used as an independent, blinded validation dataset (n = 552), designed to evaluate the model’s performance in real-world clinical scenarios. Each dataset included both HRC (non-cancer) and PDAC (cancer) samples. Samples with missing values in clinical/biochemical parameters were excluded from ML prediction analyses.

For machine learning input, we collected three data modalities: NMR-based metabolomic spectra, protein biomarker levels, and clinical/biochemical parameters. Metabolomic profiling using 600 MHz NMR with a high-throughput SampleJet system generated both 1H NMR-M (small molecule metabolites) and NMR-M+L (metabolites plus lipoproteins) spectra. These raw spectra were then processed through a standardized pipeline involving internal standard (TSP-d4) normalization, signal trimming, and water signal removal, ultimately yielding 71,074 (Supplemental Fig. 1) and 42,500 (Supplemental Fig. 2) features, respectively. Given Activin A’s reported association with early-stage PDAC and poor prognosis24,25, suggesting it plays a critical role in pancreatic cancer development. Therefore, serum Activin A level was included as a protein feature (Supplemental Fig. 3). In addition, recognizing eight clinical/biochemical parameters (age, gender, smoking, Body Mass Index (BMI), CA19-9, Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), Hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c), and fasting glucose (GluAC)) monitored by physicians may correlate with PDAC progression in high-risk individuals, so we evaluated these factors. This analysis, using Silhouette scores on UMAP clustering, identified age and CA19-9 as the variables offering the best discrimination between cancer and non-cancer cases (score: 0.35, Supplementary Fig. 4). Therefore, our final integrated dataset for model development comprised NMR-M, NMR-M+L, Activin A, age, and CA19-9 (Fig. 1A).

To handle the high dimensionality and heterogeneity of our input data, particularly the extensive spectral features (~40K-70K), we developed a multilayer support vector machine (SVM) framework (Fig. 1B, Materials and Methods). This architecture employed tailored feature selection strategies based on spectral type: SelectKBest for NMR-M and recursive feature elimination (RFE) for NMR-M+L (Supplemental Fig. 5). The resulting selected features were transformed into decision values by individual SVMs and subsequently integrated with clinical/biochemical parameters and protein features. This design aimed to prevent any single data modality from disproportionately influencing the model while retaining comprehensive spectral information, thus ensuring a balanced contribution to the prediction. The multilayer structure also enabled independent optimization and hyperparameter tuning of each SVM component before fusion, enhancing model development and flexibility.

To benchmark the performance of our multilayer SVM framework, we compared it against several established machine learning algorithms, including k-nearest neighbors (kNN), gradient boosting (GB), decision trees, random forests, and neural networks. Most of these were implemented using the AutoGluon platform, which provides robust and user-friendly ML workflows. AutoGluon’s ensemble model (14 models) utilized the same feature selection approach as our multilayer architecture (Supplemental Fig. 5). Finally, we also evaluated TabPFN, a transformer-based method incorporating attention layers and in-context learning. Due to TabPFN’s input size limitation (<500 features), we applied a modified feature selection strategy (Supplemental Fig. 6), selecting 215 features from NMR-M and 255 from NMR-M+L for integration with the clinical/biochemical parameters and protein data (Fig. 1B).

TabPFN demonstrates superior performance in PDAC detection

We evaluated the performance of various machine learning algorithms on the Developmental Test (Dev-Test) dataset. Our multilayer SVM demonstrated robust predictive capabilities, achieving an AUC of 0.96 (95% CI: 0.93–0.99), sensitivity of 0.96 (0.92–0.99), specificity of 0.83 (0.71–0.94), an overall accuracy of 0.92 (0.88–0.96), and a J-Statistic of 0.79 (0.67–0.90). Among the AutoGluon 1.1.0 models, XGBoost exhibited the highest performance, with an AUC of 0.97 (0.93–0.99) and a J-Statistic of 0.83 (0.73–0.93). TabPFN outperformed all other tested methods across nearly all metrics (Supplemental Table 1). It demonstrated high performance, achieving an AUC of 0.98 (0.94–1.00), sensitivity of 0.98 (0.95–1.00), specificity of 0.90 (0.81–0.98), accuracy of 0.96 (0.92–0.99), and a J-Statistic of 0.88 (0.78–0.96) when integrating all data modalities, while notably requiring less training time and no hyperparameter tuning.

To validate the top three Dev-Test algorithms (multilayer SVM, XGBoost, and TabPFN), we conducted a blind test and confusion matrix analysis (Fig. 2 and Table 3), which confirmed TabPFN’s superior performance. In this test, TabPFN achieved an high AUC of 0.99 (0.98–0.99), accuracy of 0.94 (0.91–0.95), sensitivity of 0.93 (0.89–0.96), and specificity of 0.94 (0.91–0.97). In contrast, the multilayer SVM and XGBoost methods were less effective, reaching overall accuracies of approximately 0.90 and 0.93, respectively. The final algorithm, named TabPFN-PanMETAI (integrating NMR metabolomics, age, CA19-9, and Activin A), demonstrated significant robustness and generalizability in the external validation test on a Lithuanian cohort (Table 2), yielding an AUC of 0.93 (0.90–0.95), sensitivity 0.90 (0.85–0.94), and specificity 0.83 (0.77–0.89), with consistent performance even for early-stage (Stage I/II) patients (Table 4). The consistent success across two geographically and behaviorally distinct populations, Taiwan and Lithuania, provides compelling evidence of TabPFN-PanMETAI’s strong potential for widespread clinical implementation.

1H NMR metabolomics in TabPFN-PanMETAI enhances early-stage PDAC detection

TabPFN-PanMETAI demonstrated high performance in the Taiwanese cohort across different PDAC stages. For detecting late-stage PDAC (III/IV), the model shown high effectiveness, achieving an accuracy of 0.95 (0.93–0.97), a sensitivity of 0.95 (0.92–0.97), a specificity of 0.95 (0.92–0.97), and an AUC of 0.99 (0.98–0.99). Importantly, TabPFN-PanMETAI also maintained high diagnostic efficacy for early-stage PDAC (I/II), achieving an accuracy of 0.92 (0.89–0.95), sensitivity of 0.78 (0.64–0.91), specificity of 0.95 (0.92–0.97), and an AUC of 0.95 (0.90–0.98) (Supplemental Table 2). Comparable results were also observed in the Lithuania cohort (Table 4). To evaluate which data modalities drove the model’s superior performance, we analyzed early and late PDAC detection using NMR metabolomics alone, clinical/biochemical parameters and protein data alone, and the fully integrated model. While our findings revealed that clinical/biochemical parameters and protein data alone were sufficient for achieving high performance in detecting late-stage (III/IV) PDAC, the integration of all data types led to a significant increase in detection sensitivity specifically for early-stage PDAC (Fig. 3 and Supplemental Table 2). This crucial result strongly supports the essential role of capturing subtle metabolic alterations within the NMR spectra, confirming that the inclusion of NMR data in TabPFN-PanMETAI is fundamental to enhancing early diagnosis.

Metabolomic Feature Selection and SHAP Analysis uncover TabPFN-PanMETAI’s Biological Insights

Given the crucial role of NMR metabolomics within TabPFN-PanMETAI for effective cancer classification, we investigated the specific features prioritized by this algorithm to gain insights into its decision-making process and enhance interpretability. To understand why NMR-based metabolomic data strengthens the model’s early predictive capabilities, we mapped the 255 and 215 metabolic features selected by TabPFN onto the 1H NMR-M+L and NMR-M spectra, respectively (Fig. 4A). The corresponding metabolite identifications are detailed in the Fig. 4 legend, revealing a total of 11 metabolites and 2 lipids from NMR-M+L, and 6 metabolites from NMR-M.

Subsequent quantification of these identified metabolites using the Bruker IVDr platform, cross-referencing with the IVDr database, revealed that 10 were quantifiable and exhibited statistically significant differences between cancer and high-risk control (HRC) groups (Fig. 4B). Notably, these metabolic alterations proved stage-dependent and align with prior research26–31. In early-stage (Stages I/II) PDAC, distinct changes were observed, including significant decreases in HDL and glutamine levels and marked elevation of lactic acid, TMAO, ornithine, glutamic acid, and glucose. In contrast, the metabolic profile became dynamic in advanced stages: some metabolites (like TMAO and Threonine) showed a trend toward normalization, while others (such as glutamic acid and glucose) remained persistently elevated. This finding highlights the dynamic role of metabolism throughout PDAC progression, emphasizing its crucial involvement in the early stages of tumor development, a pattern further confirmed by similar metabolite changes observed in the Lithuania cohort (Supplementary Fig. 7).

To further elucidate the TabPFN-PanMETAI model’s decision-making process, we performed SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis32 to assess the contribution of individual features. As depicted in Fig. 4C and Supplemental Table 3, the SHAP analysis highlighted those features at NMR-M+L ppm 1.23/3.27/3.74 (corresponding to HDL, VLDL, Glucose, TMAO, and Alanine) and NMR-M ppm 2.93/2.96 (corresponding to L-Asparagine, 3-Aminoisobutanoic acid, 2-Oxoglutaric acid, and L-Tyrosine) exerted a substantial impact on the model’s ability to distinguish PDAC from high-risk populations. These findings underscore the interpretability of the TabPFN-PanMETAI model and the biological relevance of its feature selection, bolstering its translational potential in precision medicine.

To gain deeper biological insights, we conducted metabolic pathway and interaction network analyses using MetaboAnalyst 6.0 and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA), as illustrated in Fig. 5. The metabolic pathway enrichment map (Fig. 5A) confirmed that the SHAP-annotated metabolites were significantly enriched in key dysregulated pathways in PDAC, including the Glucose-Alanine Cycle, Phenylalanine and Tyrosine Metabolism, Aspartate Metabolism, and the Malate-Aspartate Shuttle, thus reinforcing the relevance of global alterations in amino acids and energy pathways33,34. The metabolic network (Fig. 5B) further highlighted molecules such as L-glutamate, alanine, pyruvate, cholesterol, and triglycerides as central hubs of dysregulation within mitochondrial and lipid metabolism. Finally, Fig. 5C summarized the disease and biofunctions derived from the SHAP features, with top enriched categories including cancer, organismal injury, and lipid metabolism, consistent with hallmark biological themes in PDAC progression. Collectively, these multi-layered analyses support the mechanistic relevance of TabPFN-PanMETAI’s feature selection and provide crucial system-level insights into PDAC metabolic dysregulation.

Robust TabPFN performance with small datasets

Developing robust diagnostic models for low-incidence cancers like PDAC often faces the challenge of limited patient cohorts at individual centers. Traditional machine learning methods typically require large datasets for effective generalization, a constraint difficult to overcome in single-center studies. In contrast, TabPFN22 has demonstrated competitive performance on small tabular datasets without hyperparameter tuning, utilizing in-context learning from synthetic priors to approximate Bayesian inference. To assess the impact of training set size on our TabPFN-PanMETAI model’s early PDAC detection capabilities, we conducted a subsampling analysis. We randomly selected varying numbers of stage I/II PDAC patients (n = 3–199) for training and evaluated the model on an independent blind test set over 20 repetitions. Our analysis revealed a rapid improvement in model performance (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy) with increasing training sample size. Notably, TabPFN-PanMETAI achieved stable high accuracy (≈0.90) with as few as 50–70 training cases (Fig. 6, Supplemental Fig. 8). The consistent and robust performance observed with such a limited training dataset (n = 50) is remarkable. These results underscore the potential of TabPFN’s in-context learning paradigm for enabling robust diagnostic modeling in small clinical cohorts, offering a solution for medical applications where large datasets are not feasible.
paper_content.methods:
Study population
Our study analyzed a total of 1224 serum samples collected from two geographically distinct institutions: 902 from the National Taiwan University Hospital (NTUH) (January 2004–December 2022) and 322 from the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences (LSMU) (October 2015–June 2024). The study cohort was systematically partitioned to support the development and validation of machine learning. A total of 478 confirmed PDAC patients and 424 high-risk individuals (HRIs) with a family history of PDAC from Taiwan comprised the training and validation cohort, whereas 172 confirmed PDAC patients and 150 control subjects from Lithuania constituted the external validation cohort. All patients provided written informed consent prior to treatment, and diagnoses were pathologically confirmed. Samples were obtained under standardized fasting conditions and isolated from peripheral blood. This comprehensive cohort structure complies with all relevant ethical regulations, approved by both the NTUH Institutional Review Board (201301048RIND) and the Kaunas Regional Biomedical Research Ethics Committee (BE-2-31), was essential for developing a robust predictive model and validating its generalizability across diverse clinical settings (Participant demographics are detailed in Table 1 and Table 2).

Serum sample preparation
All serum samples were prepared from blood collected under fasting conditions using a serum-separating tube (BD Vacutainer Systems, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) following a standard venous blood sampling protocol. The samples were centrifuged at 3000g for 10 min at 4°C, then stored at −80°C until use. Before 1H NMR spectroscopic analysis, frozen serum samples were thawed on ice for 30 min and centrifuged for 10 min at 13000g at 4°C. Serum samples were prepared using 3 mm Ø, 5-long SampleJet NMR tubes (Brucker BioSpin GmbH, Rheinstetten, Germany). For standard sample preparation, 110 μL of serum was mixed with 110 μL phosphate buffer (75 mM Na2HPO4, 2 mM NaN3, 4·6 mM TSP in D2O), centrifuged for 10 s, and 200 μL was transferred to a 3 mm NMR tube for analyses.

1H NMR acquisition
The 1H NMR spectra were acquired using a 600 MHz Bruker Avance III HD spectrometer equipped with a 5 mm BBI probe and fitted with the Bruker SampleJet robot cooling system set to 4°C. A standard one-dimensional (1D) pulse sequence with solvent presaturation experiment included both small molecule metabolites and lipoproteins (32 scans, zero-filled to 128 K refers to NMR-M+L spectrum), whereas a Carr−Purcell−Meiboom−Gill spin−echo experiment was used to identify small molecule metabolites (32 scans, zero-filled to 128 K refers to NMR-M spectrum). The data were processed in automation using a Bruker Topspin 3·6·2 and ICON NMR to achieve phasing and baseline correction. The TSP-d4 provided a chemical shift reference (1H, δ 0·00). All spectra passed the Bruker in vitro diagnostics research (IVDr) validation criteria51—covering water suppression quality, line width (≤1.50 Hz for reference metabolite, Alanine), and shim—were included for downstream machine learning analysis.

The quantification of serum metabolites and lipoproteins were completed using the Bruker IVDr methods. A total of 39 metabolites and 112 lipoprotein parameters were generated using the IVDr Quantification in Plasma/Serum (B.I.Quant-PS) and Lipoprotein Subclass Analysis (B.I.LISA) methods52.

Data processing of 1H NMR spectra for ML
Two types of spectra (NMR-M & -M+L) were measured, one is metabolite-specific (NMR-M) and another, lipoprotein-containing (NMR-M+L). The NMR spectra were read using the nmrglue module53. A Fourier-transformed NMR spectrum contains a list of signal intensities corresponding to the 1H chemical shifts. After acquiring the reads, each spectrum was normalized by its internal standard TSP-d4 for handling bench differences. The normalized spectrum was further trimmed for removing regions that do not contain meaningful information: for NMR-M, the data with frequencies lower than or equal to 0.13 ppm, or higher than or equal to 11.13 ppm were removed; for NMR-M+L, lower than or equal to 0.11 ppm or higher than or equal to 10.00 ppm were trimmed; for both NMR spectra, data between 4.64 ppm and 4.78 ppm was removed due to the water signal. After normalization and trimming, the resulting spectra were used as inputs for the following ML pipeline.

ML Feature Selection
Each signal intensity in the spectrum is considered a separate feature. As the trimmed NMR spectrum contains 71,074 (NMR-M) and 42,500 (NMR-M+L) features, we further reduce their number using feature selection in order to extract the most relevant information.

We rank features using different methods: NMR-M with f_classif, an F-test-based algorithm, and NMR-M+L with a linear SVM, both from the scikit-learn package (version 1·2·2). Feature selection is performed using SelectKBest for NMR-M and recursive feature elimination (RFE) for NMR-M+L, both from scikit-learn. The different methods chosen for NMR-M and NMR-M+L are motivated by differences in their spectral profiles, as NMR-M+L generally contains broader signals. In order to access the discriminating power, selected features are clustered using UMAP54 [umap package (version 0.5.7)], and the Silhouette score [cuml package (version 24.10.00)] for clusters of healthy and diseased samples is calculated. With an iteration through different numbers of features picked, we searched for the features that yield the highest Silhouette score, and the corresponding features are used. With this process, we selected 1,563 features of NMR-M and 6,800 features of NMR-M+L for the multilayer SVM and AutoGluon models. For TabPFN, due to the constraints on feature numbers, we select 215 features of NMR-M and 255 features of NMR-M+L.

Missing data handling
All patients with missing or NA (Not Applicable) values in clinical/biochemical records are excluded from the dataset to provide a fair basis for benchmarking (Table S1) for all ML models. The precise numbers for each model are presented in ROC-AUC figures.

Model evaluation pipeline
The training dataset was used to train the model, and the Dev-Test was used for multilayer hyperparameters (HPs) tuning. Four indices were used to benchmark each model’s performance: accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC). After HPs tuning upon Dev-Test, the tuned models (multilayer SVM), XGBoost from AutoGluon, and TabPFN were compared, and the champion model was selected for the final performance test on the blind test dataset.

Model architectures
AutoGluon provides detailed descriptions for each of its implemented models: https://auto.gluon.ai/stable/api/autogluon.tabular.models.html23.

The description of TabPFN can be found in the original paper22.

The customized architecture for multilayer SVM is arranged to handle the multimodal nature of our inputs. This architecture is composed of 3 layers: encoder, fusion, and final decision layers.

Encoder. For multimodal learning, an “encoder” was used to transform different data modalities into a representation to fuse later. We first scaled the input data with StandardScaler function [scikit-learn package (version 1.2.2)], followed by two independent SVMs derived from the two NMR spectra with their values of radial basis function (RBF) kernel as the “decision value.” We extracted such a value from the SVM as the new representation of the original spectrum, and it was subsequently fused with clinical/biochemical parameters and protein data.

Fusion. In general, there are several methods for fusing modalities in multimodal learning. Here, we simply chose to concatenate the data. Following the encoder layer, the decision values were concatenated with clinical/biochemical parameters and protein data.

Final decision. The concatenated features were scaled again using StandardScaler, followed by another SVM for the final decisions.

Measurement of Activin A levels in serum
Serum levels of Activin A were quantified using commercially available sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay kits (DAC00B, R&D Systems, Inc.) based on the manufacturer’s instructions. Assays were performed duplicate for both biomarkers. Activin A levels were measured after a twofold dilution of the serum samples, followed by absorbance measurement at 450 nm with the same spectrophotometer. Activin A data is presented as pg/mg, which was normalized to the total protein (mg/mL) in the serum sample.

Statistical analysis
The biochemical results are presented as the means and standard deviations. They were analyzed according to the statistical methods available in GraphPad Prism 10·0 (San Diego, CA). Most metrics in ML models are neither normally distributed (confirmed by Kolmogorov–Smirnov test) nor having an equal variance (confirmed by Levene test), we performed Wilcoxon Signed Rank test to tackle this data distribution. All statistical tests were performed using the stats module from the SciPy library (version 1.14.1). Significant differences were presented with P-values < 0·05.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Summary:
This paper presents PanMETAI, a tabular foundation model based on TabPFN, developed for the accurate and early
detection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) using ¹H NMR metabolomics, clinical data (age, CA19-9), and the
protein biomarker Activin A. The study encompasses 902 participants and employs a three-tier data division (training,
development, and blind test) to build and validate models, including multilayer SVM, AutoGluon-XGBoost, and TabPFN.
PanMETAI demonstrates outstanding diagnostic performance (AUC up to 0.99, accuracy ~94%), particularly in early-stage
detection, and proves robust even with small datasets. The study includes feature interpretability via SHAP analysis and
metabolite quantification, positioning PanMETAI as a non-invasive, scalable diagnostic aid.
Positives:
1- The paper impressively integrates NMR spectral features with clinical and biomarker data, addressing a real-world
challenge in early cancer diagnostics.
2- PanMETAI, leveraging TabPFN, exhibits high accuracy and robustness with small training sets, a notable advancement
for low-incidence disease modelling.
3- The inclusion of SHAP analysis and biochemical quantification adds transparency and scientific validity, enhancing
translational relevance.
Negatives:
- All data is derived from a single institution, limiting generalizability. Cross-center or international cohorts would strengthen
the conclusions.
- While feature selection methods are described, the rationale for specific thresholds and their reproducibility across cohorts
is not clearly justified.
Major points:
- While TabPFN is presented as the foundation of the PanMETAI framework, the manuscript provides limited justification for
its selection over other high-performing tabular models such as TabNet or FT-Transformer. Although the results are
impressive, a more critical discussion is warranted to contextualize TabPFN’s advantages—particularly its in-context
learning paradigm—in relation to PDAC’s clinical constraints. The model’s parameter-free nature and efficiency are
acknowledged, but the novelty would be more compelling if benchmarked against a broader spectrum of foundation models,
especially those designed for biological datasets.
- The study highlights metabolite-level changes and uses SHAP for feature attribution, but it stops short of performing deeper
biological pathway analysis or metabolic network interpretation. Mapping the identified features to disrupted biochemical
pathways (e.g., glutaminolysis, glycolysis, lipid remodelling) could significantly enhance the translational relevance of the
findings. Without this layer of biological insight, the model’s interpretability, while technically sound, remains disconnected
from systems-level understanding of PDAC progression.
- Several methodological gaps limit the robustness and generalizability of the model. First, no ablation study is performed to
assess the individual contribution of each data modality or feature subset, which is crucial for clinical simplification. Second,
although the data spans nearly two decades (2004–2022), the analysis does not investigate how diagnostic markers or
model performance may vary over time, missing an opportunity to explore cohort drift or biomarker stability. Lastly, external
validation using data from other institutions or populations is absent, significantly limiting clinical readiness claims.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors use an MR spec serum signature of metabolites and lipoproteins along with CA19-9 and Activin A as a test for
pancreatic cancer and show that it achieves high performance in a validation set.
One limitation of the study is the age difference between the cases and controls, with a mean of ~15 years. The controls
were patients with familial/genetic risk. Although this difference is not likely to dramatically affect the results, certain
metabolic alterations increase with age, such as impaired glucose tolerance/DM and associated changes in lipids that could
modify the prediction. In addition, the number of stage I/II PDAC cases in the validation set is also quite small compared to
the number of Stage III/IV cases; 37 vs 241. Therefore, the diagnostic performance of the model is driven by advanced-stage
cases, which is not an adequate test of model performance.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This study presents PanMETAI, a transformer-based AI model (TabPFN) that integrates NMR metabolomics, clinical data
(including age and CA19-9), and protein biomarkers (Activin A) for the diagnosis of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
(PDAC). Using 902 serum samples from high-risk controls and PDAC patients across different stages, the model achieved
outstanding performance (AUC 0.99, accuracy 0.94) on a blinded validation cohort. Notably, PanMETAI improved early-
stage detection and remained robust with small sample sizes, highlighting its potential for clinical deployment in low-
incidence cancer diagnostics.
The choice of NMR as the primary metabolomics platform, while well justified in terms of throughput and quantitative
reproducibility, may limit the detection of low-abundance yet biologically relevant metabolites due to its lower sensitivity and
narrower dynamic range compared to high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS). Although the authors briefly mention
some challenges associated with MS, it would strengthen the manuscript to provide a more balanced discussion. HRMS-
based metabolomics, particularly in targeted and semi-targeted formats, has evolved significantly, with robust
standardization protocols, high analytical sensitivity, and broad metabolite coverage. It remains a leading platform for the
discovery of cancer biomarkers. The authors should clarify why HRMS was omitted and whether future iterations of
PanMETAI might integrate MS-based data to further enhance the model’s diagnostic utility.
Major Methodological Concern: Sample Preparation for NMR Spectroscopy
A critical limitation of this study lies in the serum sample preparation protocol used for ^1H NMR metabolomics. The
manuscript describes a direct dilution of native serum with phosphate buffer in D₂O (110 µL + 110 µL), but fails to address
the presence of intact serum proteins such as albumin and globulins. These macromolecules dominate the NMR spectrum
and broaden signals of low-molecular-weight metabolites through T₂ relaxation and line broadening effects. Without protein
removal, either by organic solvent precipitation (e.g., methanol or acetonitrile) or ultrafiltration (e.g., with a 3 kDa or 10 kDa
cutoff), the spectra are likely compromised, thereby undermining the accuracy and sensitivity of metabolite detection.
Although the authors mention using CPMG sequences for metabolite detection, this is not a substitute for protein removal.
CPMG suppresses broad macromolecular signals but does not eliminate their interference, especially in crowded regions of
the spectrum or when quantification is required.
Further, the use of a 1:1 dilution with phosphate buffer introduces significant concerns:
• Dilution reduces signal intensity, particularly affecting low-abundance biomarkers.
• Na₂HPO₄ can alter the chemical environment of pH-sensitive metabolites (e.g., citrate, lactate).
• The preparation does not eliminate water, despite D₂O use. Without a detailed description of presaturation parameters,
water suppression quality, or the management of residual water signals, it is difficult to assess the reliability of the spectra.
This lack of standard protein-removal procedures represents a fundamental methodological flaw. Without addressing this
issue, the validity of the downstream machine learning models, however robust, remains questionable, as they are ultimately
trained on spectra that may be distorted or biased by macromolecular contributions.
Recommendation: The authors must either (1) repeat the NMR acquisition using appropriate protein-removal protocols or (2)
provide quantitative evidence (e.g., metabolite linewidths, S/N ratios, validation via IVDr) that the current preparation yields
high-quality, interpretable spectra free from macromolecular interference.
1. Validity: The experimental design for the AI analysis is rigorous and methodologically sound. The use of a blind validation
cohort (n = 552) is a significant strength, and the data preprocessing and normalization steps are clearly described. Feature
selection strategies were appropriately adapted to different data modalities. TabPFN’s performance was benchmarked
against multiple algorithms (SVM, AutoGluon/XGBoost), and statistical evaluations were conducted using appropriate
metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and Wilcoxon test). The rationale for focusing on age and CA19-9 as the clinical
variables included in the final model is supported by clustering analysis (using Silhouette scores and UMAP), which
indicates that they provide the highest discriminatory power. However, given that other variables, such as HbA1c, BMI, and
fasting glucose, also show statistically significant differences between groups (Table 1), a brief clarification in the text would
reinforce why these variables were ultimately excluded despite their apparent univariate significance.
2. Significance: The work is highly significant and timely. It addresses a major challenge in oncology: the early detection of
PDAC, a disease with a poor prognosis and no reliable screening test. The use of AI to integrate complex NMR
metabolomic signatures with minimal clinical data is innovative, and the demonstrated performance across disease stages
(especially early-stage) is clinically meaningful. The minimal data requirement (n = 50 - 70) for robust prediction is especially
impactful for rare diseases.
3. Data and Methodology: The NMR data acquisition and preprocessing pipeline is clearly described and appears to meet
high standards in terms of automation and technical reproducibility (e.g., CV <1.4% for sample handling). The feature
selection and machine learning workflow is transparent and technically well executed, and the use of SHAP analysis adds
interpretability to the model by identifying key biological signals.
However, a major methodological flaw lies in the sample preparation protocol. The authors do not perform any protein
removal (e.g., via precipitation or ultrafiltration), which is a critical step in serum metabolomics. Without this, macromolecules
such as albumin and globulins are retained in the sample, potentially distorting the ^1H NMR spectrum by line broadening
and baseline interference. This can significantly affect the quantification of low-molecular-weight metabolites, even with the
use of CPMG sequences. This omission may undermine the reliability of the downstream analysis and classification
performance.
4. Analytical Approach: The authors developed and compared multiple machine learning architectures, including a custom
multilayer SVM, AutoGluon ensemble models (e.g., XGBoost), and TabPFN, each trained using distinct feature selection
strategies tailored to the spectral characteristics of the NMR data. For example, SelectKBest was applied to NMR-M
features, and recursive feature elimination (RFE) was applied to NMR-M+L (pp. 9–10; Methods, lines 461–469). A reduced
subset of features (215 and 255, respectively) was used to accommodate the dimensional constraints of TabPFN (line 478).
Hyperparameter tuning was performed on the development set for the SVM and AutoGluon models, whereas TabPFN
required no tuning, relying instead on its in-context learning framework, which was trained on synthetic priors (line 297- 299).
This TabPFN approach represents a novel transformer-based solution capable of producing accurate predictions from small
datasets (an essential strength in the context of rare cancers like PDAC). The authors evaluated model performance using
standard classification metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, accuracy) and confidence intervals derived from bootstrap
resampling (Table 2). However, the manuscript would benefit from the inclusion of additional metrics such as F1 scores,
precision-recall curves, or calibration plots, which are particularly valuable in diagnostic applications with class imbalance or
varying prevalence.
Suggested Improvements
Expand discussion on (i) generalizability across ethnicities and different patient cohorts. (ii) Limitations regarding metabolite
identification from NMR alone (e.g., peak overlap).
Clarify exclusion criteria for clinical features.
Consider including or referencing external validation efforts (if any are planned) or providing discussion on feasibility.
Include full SHAP feature names in visualizations.
Explicitly state which SHAP or statistical features were most relevant to early vs. late-stage detection (currently inferred but
not quantitatively ranked).
5. Clarity and Context: The manuscript is clearly written, accessible to readers across disciplines, and well contextualized
with current literature. The introduction and discussion provide a balanced overview of the PDAC diagnostic landscape,
highlighting gaps and justifying the proposed approach. The figures are informative, although Figure 5 would benefit from
enhanced visual clarity and explanation.
Importantly, the figure captions are not clearly presented in the main body or as a standalone figure legend section, making it
difficult to interpret the figures independently of the text. For a manuscript of this complexity, full, self-contained figure
legends are essential to ensure clarity.
6. References: The manuscript cites relevant and recent work, including foundational studies in metabolomics, AI-based
diagnostics, and PDAC biology. The references are comprehensive and appropriate.
7. Expertise Scope: The evaluation was performed from the perspective of expertise in sample preparation, clinical
metabolomics, diagnostic model development, and translational oncology. While the reviewer did not independently verify
the TabPFN implementation or code, the methods appear to be appropriately adapted from the cited sources and aligned
with current best practices in AI model development. However, based on established protocols in serum metabolomics, a
major methodological concern arises from the sample preparation workflow, which does not include any step for protein
removal (e.g., ultrafiltration or precipitation). This omission is likely to result in compromised spectral quality due to
macromolecular interference, raising questions about the reliability of downstream metabolite quantification and model
performance. This issue must be addressed for the study’s conclusions to be fully validated.

Detailed response to reviewers’ comments
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Summary:
This paper presents PanMETAI, a tabular foundation model based on TabPFN, developed for
the accurate and early detection of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) using ¹HNMR
metabolomics, clinical data (age, CA19-9), and the protein biomarker Activin A. The study
encompasses 902 participants and employs a three-tier data division (training, development,
and blind test) to build and validate models, including multilayer SVM, AutoGluon-XGBoost,
and TabPFN. PanMETAI demonstrates outstanding diagnostic performance (AUC up to 0.99,
accuracy ~94%), particularly in early-stage detection, and proves robust even with small
datasets. The study includes feature interpretability via SHAP analysis and metabolite
quantification, positioning PanMETAI as a non-invasive, scalable diagnostic aid.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s positive comments and encouragement.
Comments:
Comment 1. Positives:
1- The paper impressively integrates NMR spectral features with clinical and biomarker data,
addressing a real-world challenge in early cancer diagnostics.
2- PanMETAI, leveraging TabPFN, exhibits high accuracy and robustness with small training
sets, a notable advancement for low-incidence disease modelling.
3- The inclusion of SHAP analysis and biochemical quantification adds transparency and
scientific validity, enhancing translational relevance.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s recognition.
Negatives:
Comment 2.
1. All data is derived from a single institution, limiting generalizability. Cross-center or
international cohorts would strengthen the conclusions.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In response, we have expanded our
validation to include an independent serum cohort collected from a geographically distinct
European population at the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences, to assess the model’s
generalizability across different countries and centers. This external cohort (N= 322) comprised
150 high-risk controls (HRC), 62 patients with early-stage pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
(PDAC, stages I/II), and 110 patients with advanced-stage PDAC (stages III/IV).
Remarkably, the PanMETAI model demonstrated robust predictive performance in this
external international cohort, achieving an AUC of 0.93, 90% sensitivity, and 83% specificity
in detecting patients with PDAC. This performance was consistently maintained in stage I/II
patients, with an AUC of 0.91, 84% sensitivity, and 83% specificity (see New Table 3). These
findings not only underscore the reproducibility of the PanMETAI model across different
populations and institutions but also highlight its potential clinical utility for diagnosing PDAC
in diverse populations with varying dietary habits in response to different real-world settings.
Corresponding changes in the revised manuscript:
● Page 3, Abstract section, Lines 83-87: We added the description of the European
validation cohort performance.
● Page 7, Results section, Lines 227-234: We added the description of the European
validation cohort and the model performance of PanMETAI.
● Page 10, Discussion, Lines 358-361: Discussion of the generalizability of PanMETAI
model.
● Revised Table 1: Characterization for PDAC and HRC in the 3rd external validation
cohort from Lithuania.
● New Table 3: List the performance metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, F1 score) of
the PanMETAI model evaluated in the 3rd external Lithuania cohort.

patients and high-risk controls (HRC) in the 1st exploration, 2nd validation, and 3rd external
validation cohorts.
Table 3. Diagnostic performance of PanMETAI in the external Lithuanian’s cohort (N=322).
Comment 3.
2. While feature selection methods are described, the rationale for specific thresholds and their
reproducibility across cohorts is not clearly justified.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer's insightful question regarding our feature selection methodology
and its reproducibility. We agree that the rationale behind feature selection thresholds is a
critical aspect of model development. We would like to clarify our approach and the underlying
logic behind it.
Our study was meticulously designed with two distinct cohorts: the exploration cohort
(Cohort 1) and the independent validation cohort (Cohort 2). We want to emphasize that
Cohort 2 was isolated entirely during the model development process, with no data from it used
for training, hyperparameter tuning, or feature selection. This strategy was specifically
employed to prevent data leakage and over-fitting, ensuring a robust, unbiased final validation.
Rationale for Feature Selection & Thresholds
In our machine learning pipeline, feature selection is viewed as an integral part of the overall
model optimization process, rather than a separate, fixed step. The thresholds for feature
selection (e.g., the number of features to select, K in SelectKBest) are treated as
hyperparameters. The optimal number of features is determined by maximizing the model's
performance on the development dataset, specifically its performance on the developing test
set. This approach ensures that we select the most informative and predictive features for our
specific modeling task.
For example, we used the Silhouette score to evaluate the clustering quality of the selected
features. The threshold (i.e., the number of features) that resulted in the highest Silhouette score
was chosen because it provided the best separation between the cancer and non-cancer groups.
This is a data-driven approach, not an arbitrary one.
Reproducibility Across Cohorts
We understand the reviewer's concern about reproducibility. However, reproducibility of the
feature selection process itself across different cohorts is not an expected outcome, nor is it the
primary goal. Each cohort, particularly those from diverse populations, may exhibit unique
biological and demographic characteristics. A well-designed feature selection pipeline should
identify the most relevant features for the data it is trained on.
Instead, the accurate measure of our model's robustness and the quality of our chosen features
lie in its predictive performance on an independent validation cohort. The fact that our
model, trained in using features and thresholds optimized on Cohort 1, achieved excellent
performance on the completely unseen Cohort 2 already validates the robustness and
generalizability of our selected features. It demonstrates that the metabolic and clinical
signatures identified in Cohort 1 are not specific to that cohort but are generalizable markers
for pancreatic cancer.
Comment 4. Major points:
1. While TabPFN is presented as the foundation of the PanMETAI framework, the manuscript
provides limited justification for its selection over other high-performing tabular models such
as TabNet or FT-Transformer.
2. Although the results are impressive, a more critical discussion is warranted to contextualize
TabPFN’s advantages—particularly its in-context learning paradigm—in relation to PDAC’s
clinical constraints.
3. The model’s parameter-free nature and efficiency are acknowledged, but the novelty would
be more compelling if benchmarked against a broader spectrum of foundation models,
especially those designed for biological datasets.
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the suggestions.
(1 & 3) TabNet (Ref 1) was excluded due to its known sensitivity to hyperparameter settings,
the need for preprocessing (e.g., handling missing values via imputation), and comparatively
slow tuning and training times relative to alternatives. It requires tuning of more than eight
hyperparameters (25 formally), making it more suitable for medium to large datasets where the
risk of overfitting is lower. In contrast, TabPFN—designed for tabular classification on smaller
datasets—is pre-trained, requires no tuning, and has been shown to consistently outperform
boosted tree models and neural methods (including TabNet) on OpenML benchmarks with
≤ 1,000 samples (TabPFN paper), executing inference within seconds. Although TabNet offers
fine-grained interpretability via attention masks, this was deemed insufficient to justify its
inclusion, given TabPFN’s higher accuracy, native support for missing values, and
substantially lower setup complexity.
However, in order to further strengthen our benchmark, we chose to add the FT-transformer
(Ref 2) into our benchmarks, as it requires fewer hyperparameters than TabNet; we didn’t find
a systematic comparison for the FT-transformer with TabPFN, and it is generally more stable
and easier to tune than TabNet, especially on small datasets (Ref 2). We added a performance
test for the FT-transformer for our benchmark.

Response:
First– Ablation study not performed
We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion regarding ablation analysis. As shown in
Supplemental Table 2, we conducted an ablation study to evaluate the relative contribution of
individual data modalities (NMR metabolomics-only vs. protein and clinical-only vs. 3
combinations) for both early- and late-stage analyses. Results revealed that the metabolomics
data alone or clinical/protein data alone already achieved an acceptable diagnostic performance
(AUC >0.8 in early-stage and AUC > 0.9 in late-stage), while the integration with
metabolomics, protein (Activin A), and clinical features (CA19-9) further enhanced robustness
and especially improved the sensitivity in the stage I/II of PDAC prediction. This finding
supports the essential of combining both up-down omics study (from protein to metabolomics
data) to enhance early diagnosis in real-world settings.

sensitivity (accuracy among these PDAC patients) across all 18 years, and no significant impact
was observed in our model’s performance. These findings suggest that the features employed
by the PanMETAI model are temporally stable.

a future goal following an investigation of the addressed metabolites from SHAP analysis.

Comment 2. The choice of NMR as the primary metabolomics platform, while well justified
in terms of throughput and quantitative reproducibility, may limit the detection of low-
abundance yet biologically relevant metabolites due to its lower sensitivity and narrower
dynamic range compared to high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS). Although the authors
briefly mention some challenges associated with MS, it would strengthen the manuscript to
provide a more balanced discussion. HRMS-based metabolomics, particularly in targeted and
semi-targeted formats, has evolved significantly, with robust standardization protocols, high
analytical sensitivity, and broad metabolite coverage. It remains a leading platform for the
discovery of cancer biomarkers. The authors should clarify why HRMS was omitted and
whether future iterations of PanMETAI might integrate MS-based data to further enhance the
model’s diagnostic utility.
Response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments. We agree that HRMS-based
metabolomics is a powerful platform for detecting low-abundance metabolites and has indeed
advanced significantly in standardization, sensitivity, and metabolome coverage. However, in
the context of clinical biomarker discovery and model translation, we prioritized NMR
spectroscopy due to its superior reproducibility, throughput, and quantitative consistency,
particularly critical in large-scale cohort studies. Reproducibility remains a key factor for
biomarker reliability and clinical applicability.
Furthermore, our whole-spectrum profiling strategy with NMR does not rely solely on
metabolite identification or quantification. Instead, it leverages the entire spectral feature space,
including those signals below quantification limits but over the limit of detection. This
approach allows effective utilization of all available biochemical signals for machine learning-
based model training, enhancing the coverage of NMR-based metabolomics.
Nonetheless, we fully acknowledge the complementary value of MS-based platforms. In fact,
we are actively pursuing HRMS-based quantitative metabolomics to identify additional
candidate metabolites for PDAC detection. However, we have encountered substantial
challenges in signal reproducibility, particularly for those small metabolites across datasets,
which currently hinders direct integration into diagnostic models.
In line with the reviewer’s suggestion and inspired by literature reporting selected lipid species,
such as very long-chain sphingomyelins, ceramides, and (lyso)phosphatidylcholines, as
promising diagnostic biomarkers (Wolrab, D., et al., Ref 1) for pancreatic cancer. Therefore,
we plan to integrate HRMS-based lipidomics in future iterations of PanMETAI to enhance
model performance potentially. This future direction for integration of HRMS-based
lipidomics has now been included in the revised Discussion section to reflect its importance.

Comment 3. Major Methodological Concern: Sample Preparation for NMR
Spectroscopy
A critical limitation of this study lies in the serum sample preparation protocol used for^1H
NMR metabolomics. The manuscript describes a direct dilution of native serum with phosphate
buffer in D₂O (110 μL + 110 μL), but fails to address the presence of intact serum proteins such
as albumin and globulins. These macromolecules dominate the NMR spectrum and broaden
signals of low-molecular-weight metabolites through T₂ relaxation and line broadening effects.
Without protein removal, either by organic solvent precipitation (e.g., methanol or acetonitrile)
or ultrafiltration (e.g., with a 3 kDa or 10 kDa cutoff), the spectra are likely compromised,
thereby undermining the accuracy and sensitivity of metabolite detection. Although the authors
mention using CPMG sequences for metabolite detection, this is not a substitute for protein
removal. CPMG suppresses broad macromolecular signals but does not eliminate their
interference, especially in crowded regions of the spectrum or when quantification is required.
Further, the use of a 1:1 dilution with phosphate buffer introduces significant concerns:•
Dilution reduces signal intensity, particularly affecting low-abundance biomarkers.• Na₂HPO₄
can alter the chemical environment of pH-sensitive metabolites (e.g., citrate, lactate).• The
preparation does not eliminate water, despite D₂O use. Without a detailed description of
presaturation parameters, water suppression quality, or the management of residual water
signals, it is difficult to assess the reliability of the spectra.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comment regarding serum sample preparation. While
protein precipitation or ultrafiltration is commonly employed in certain metabolomics
workflows, our NMR-based approach follows a well-established and validated protocol that
retains serum macromolecules. Specifically, the method aligns with the standardized
procedures recommended by Bruker IVDr, which are widely adopted in large-scale NMR
metabolomics and diagnostic studies. This protocol has been consistently shown to yield robust
and reproducible quantification of low-molecular-weight metabolites even in the presence of
macromolecules, particularly when using CPMG pulse sequences to suppress broad signals
from proteins and lipoproteins. Importantly, this approach has been validated in high-impact
studies across diverse disease areas, including:
1. Zhou et al., Adv Sci, 2024 (Ref 1)
2. Karjalainen et al., Nature, 2024 (Ref2)
3. Fromentin et al., Nat Med, 2022 (Ref3)
According to Bruker’s technical report, this protocol has been applied in over 230 peer-
reviewed publications across various disease areas since 2017.
In addition, another advantage of preserving serum protein content allows us to perform
simultaneous analysis of lipoprotein subclass profiles (NMR-M+L spectra), an important
feature for pancreatic cancer research. (Ref 4) Lastly, retaining macromolecules also facilitates
direct spectral comparison and data integration with other research centers that employing the
same NMR methodology.
We agree that CPMG is not a complete substitute for physical protein removal, but in the
context of standardized and harmonized NMR-based diagnostics, our approach provides a
practical and validated balance between metabolomic resolution and clinical feasibility.
Regarding water suppression and spectral quality:
All acquired spectra passed Buker IVDr QC criteria for experiment validation, including water

methodologically sound. The use of a blind validation cohort (n = 552) is a significant strength,
and the data preprocessing and normalization steps are clearly described. Feature selection
strategies were appropriately adapted to different data modalities. TabPFN’s performance was

evaluations were conducted using appropriate metrics (AUC, sensitivity, specificity, and
Wilcoxon test). The rationale for focusing on age and CA19-9 as the clinical variables included
in the final model is supported by clustering analysis (using Silhouette scores and UMAP),
which indicates that they provide the highest discriminatory power. However, given that other
variables, such as HbA1c, BMI, and fasting glucose, also show statistically significant
differences between groups (Table 1), a brief clarification in the text would reinforce why these
variables were ultimately excluded despite their apparent univariate significance.
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer's detailed attention to our feature selection process. This is an
important point for clarifying the distinction between raw statistical significance and utility in
a predictive model. Although variables like HbA1c, BMI, and fasting glucose showed
statistically significant differences between groups (as seen in Table 1), they were ultimately
excluded from the final PanMETAI model for two primary, methodologically sound reasons:
a. Data Completeness and Clinical Monitoring Standard: The high rate of missing or
incomplete data for HbA1c, BMI, and fasting glucose within our broader clinical records made
them unsuitable for reliable feature inclusion across the entire cohort. We prioritized Age and
CA19-9 because they are robustly and consistently collected as standard monitoring parameters
for PDAC, thus ensuring maximum data completeness.
b. Fair Benchmarking of AI Models: Excluding features with high missingness was
necessary to establish a fair baseline for comparing TabPFN against traditional machine
learning methods (such as SVM and XGBoost/AutoGluon). While TabPFN inherently has
capabilities to handle missing data, most benchmark models do not. Relying on incomplete
data would have unfairly compromised the performance of our comparison models, thereby
undermining the rigor of our entire benchmarking effort.
In summary, the decision to rely exclusively on Age and CA19-9 was justified not only by the
superior discriminant power observed in the UMAP/Silhouette analysis but also by the
critical need for data completeness to maintain methodological integrity when validating the
TabPFN platform.

Response:
We thank the reviewer for the critical evaluation of our methodology and for highlighting the
importance of protein removal in serum metabolomics.
We want to clarify that our sample preparation strategy was intentional and adheres to
established protocols for clinical metabolomics studies, specifically those designed for large-
scale, high-throughput diagnostic applications.
a. Clinical Rationale (IVD-Grade Protocol): Our study intentionally employs a minimal
sample preparation approach that aligns with IVD-grade (In Vitro Diagnostic) clinical NMR
protocols (specifically the Bruker IVDr platform). These protocols are standardized to
maximize reproducibility and retain the maximal biological information present in the serum,
including signals from lipoproteins and larger molecules. Removing all proteins, while
simplifying the spectrum, would eliminate valuable diagnostic information related to
lipoprotein profiles that we utilize in our multi-modal approach.
b. Addressing Macromolecular Interference: We recognize that macromolecules (like
albumin) can interfere with small-molecule metabolite quantification. However, this
interference is mitigated by two key technical factors:
CPMG Pulse Sequences: We utilized the Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) pulse
sequence for the NMR-M (small metabolite) spectrum. This sequence effectively suppresses
the broad signals from macromolecules, thereby isolating and enhancing the signals from the
small, mobile metabolites.
Rigorous QC: Our data underwent stringent quality control checks, including those validated
by the IVDr platform, which cover essential parameters such as metabolite linewidths and
signal-to-noise ratios to support the efficiency of CPMG pulse sequences.
The successful performance of our model, benchmarked against external validation cohorts and
supported by robust QC data (e.g., CV < 1.4% for handling), indicates that our methodological
choices did not compromise the reliability of the downstream classification performance.
This minimal preparation strategy is a methodological feature that enhances the translational
potential of PanMETAI, as it enables rapid and standardized screening in a clinical setting.

Response 12:
We thank the reviewer for their rigorous review, particularly their acknowledgment of the
study's methodological soundness in AI analysis, the strength of using a blinded validation
cohort, and the appropriate adaptation of methods from cited sources. We also appreciate the
reviewer's identification of the specific concern regarding our sample preparation protocol.
We would like to clarify that our minimal sample preparation approach was intentional and
aligns with standardized protocols designed for high-throughput clinical applications, although
we acknowledge the theoretical risks of macromolecular interference.
a. Alignment with Clinical Standards (IVD-Grade Protocol): Our protocol follows the
standard established by the Bruker IVDr (In Vitro Diagnostic Research) platform. This
minimal preparation method is a deliberate choice in large-scale clinical metabolomics,
designed to maximize standardization and reproducibility—crucial factors for clinical
deployment—while retaining the maximum biological information, including signals from
lipoproteins and associated small molecules.
b. Technical Mitigation of Interference: We successfully mitigated the impact of
macromolecular interference (e.g., from albumin) through the use of specific NMR sequences:
The CPMG (Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill) pulse sequence was employed explicitly for the
NMR-M spectrum to effectively suppress broad macromolecular signals and isolate small,
mobile metabolites.
The overall data quality was confirmed by passing the IVDr platform's stringent Quality
Control (QC) criteria, which validate essential parameters such as metabolite linewidths and
signal-to-noise ratios.
The fact that our model, trained on data prepared using this method, achieved outstanding
performance (AUC 0.99) on an independent external validation cohort strongly suggests that
the methodological choice did not undermine the reliability of the downstream
classification performance.
We believe this approach enhances the translational viability of PanMETAI, as it relies on a
rapid, standardized protocol compatible with clinical laboratory workflows. We will clarify
this rationale in the revised manuscript to ensure the conclusion is fully validated in the context
of our translational aims.

We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the limitations of CA9-9,
especially in early-stage and asymptomatic PDAC. Indeed, CA19-9 is not an ideal standalone
biomarker for early detection of PDAC, where its sensitivity is limited. However, in our clinical
feature selection analysis, CA19-9 demonstrated a high silhouette score, indicating strong
discriminatory power in combination with age among the clinical variables assessed (see
Supplemental Figure 4). Therefore, we included CA19-9 as one of the diagnostic components
in our PanMETAI model. Moreover, our ablation analysis (see Supplemental Table 2)
revealed that combining CA19-9 with metabolic features and Activin A protein levels
significantly improved the overall diagnostic performance of the model compared to a single
metabolic modality alone. This finding supports the rationale for incorporating CA19-9 into an
integrated diagnostic strategy, rather than relying on it in isolation. Together, these results
highlight the added value of a multimodal biomarker approach in improving diagnostic
accuracy for PDAC, particularly in high-risk populations.
Additionally, we condensed the discussion section, which was repetitive, and included the
strengths/ limitations of this study to further enhance the comprehensive understanding of
pancreatic cancer research.
(i) NMR-based metabolomics approach:
Strengths. NMR-based approach adheres to well-established and standardized protocol
recommended by the Bruker IVDr platform, which is widely adopted in large-scale
metabolomics and clinical diagnostic studies. This standardization not only facilitates future
data integration and cross-center comparability but also enables the concurrent analysis of lipid
profiles, thereby enhancing the robustness and translational potential of our findings.
Limitations. While SHAP-based annotation revealed distinct metabolic associations between
early- and late-stage pancreatic cancer, enabling subsequent pathway and network analyses
(Figure 5), the underlying biological mechanisms remain speculative and require further
validation. Moreover, inherent technical limitations of 1H NMR spectroscopy, particularly in
resolving overlapping signals in crowded spectral regions, can constrain the confident
identifications of specific lipid species. To address these challenges, future iterations of the
PanMETAI model will integrate complementary mass spectroscopy-based lipidomic profiling.
These additions aim to expand the metabolite coverage and further enhance diagnostic
performance, especially for those lipids such as long-chain sphingomyelins, ceramides, and
(lyso)phosphatidylcholines have been reported as informative biomarkers for pancreatic cancer
(Ref 1).
(ii) TabPFN-based PanMETAI model:
Strengths. One of the main strengths of TabPFN is its ability to perform in-context learning.
Once pre-trained, it makes predictions for new datasets in a single forward pass, without
requiring additional optimization or hyperparameter tuning. This eliminates the need to
repeatedly search for optimal hyperparameters when training data is obtained from different
institutions with slight variations in experimental methods. Additionally, TabPFN is robust to
missing values and outliers, and emerging studies suggest it can also handle certain
distributional shifts (Ref 2). For classification and regression tasks involving up to 10,000
samples and 500 features, TabPFN consistently outperforms tuned gradient-boosted decision
trees (e.g., CatBoost, LightGBM), deep tabular models (e.g., FT-Transformer), and AutoML
systems such as AutoGluon (Ref 3).
Limitations. However, it is designed primarily for smaller datasets, and its performance,
latency, and memory consumption degrade significantly beyond 10,000 samples or 500
features. While methods to extend to larger datasets do exist (Ref 4) we haven’t implemented
them as we observe sufficient performance. Another limitation is, although TabPFN integrates
with SHAP and Leave-One-Covariate-Out (LOCO) for interpretability, the Transformer-based
architecture remains less interpretable than traditional models like decision trees or linear
regression (Ref 5).
